summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in São Tomé and Príncipe since the Penal Code entered into force in November 2012, and the age of consent is set equally at 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. One source states that Law 15/2021 raised the age of consent to 18 for everyone in 2021, which would apply to visitors as well as residents; the sources disagree on the current figure.

São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal framework for gender-identity recognition. There is no procedure for amending sex or gender markers on identity documents, so a traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation should expect the mismatch to be visible to border and hotel officials with no domestic remedy behind it.

No form of relationship recognition exists for same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, and same-sex couples cannot adopt.

Protection against discrimination is narrow. Article 16.2 of the 2019 Labour Code prohibits discrimination in employment on grounds of sexual orientation, and no broader general anti-discrimination statute covers housing, services or public accommodation. Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code permits enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by hatred of a person's sexual orientation, a provision that on its face addresses bias-motivated violence.

The state has signed the United Nations joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity, placing its official position on record in favour of decriminalisation and non-discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
A 2016 poll found that 46% of São Toméans would not object to an LGBTQ neighbour, a measure of public attitudes rather than of legal protection and one that predates the current decade.

The islands are small, peaceful and receiving growing tourist traffic, which shapes the practical environment for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor: limited anonymity, a thin expatriate and community infrastructure, and few places to withdraw to if a confrontation occurs.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the 2019 Labour Code ban on sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, and by the Penal Code's enhanced-sentencing provision for bias-motivated crimes. These are the only statutory protections in force.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, no access to relationship recognition or joint adoption, and no general anti-discrimination coverage outside the workplace.

The age of consent applies equally to all orientations and gender identities; sources give it as 16 under the 2012 Penal Code and as 18 under Law 15/2021.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents incidents of violence against transgender people in São Tomé and Príncipe, their dates, or any police or judicial outcome, so the level of such violence is unresolved rather than established as low.

Nothing in the sources addresses airport or border screening of gender markers, entry or visa rules that turn on gender presentation, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or restroom and facility rules. These remain not sourced.

The current age of consent is stated inconsistently across the sources (16 versus 18); the discrepancy is unresolved and should be checked against the text of Law 15/2021.

Enforcement of the Labour Code's sexual-orientation clause and of the Penal Code's bias-motivation sentencing enhancement is not evidenced by any case or complaint data in the inventory.
